d: a unit measuring exposure to x-rays or gamma rays
s: The physicist recorded the dose in roentgen units after every measurement.
r: Named for Wilhelm Roentgen (1845-1923), who discovered X-rays in 1895
h: ROENTGEN keeps the German OE pair — RO-ENT-GEN, never plain RENT.

d: to cut passages thought improper out of a book or play
s: Editors used to bowdlerize the play before schoolchildren were allowed to read it.
r: Named for Thomas Bowdler (1754-1825), who published an expurgated Shakespeare
h: BOWDLERIZE keeps the silent W of BOWL — BOWD-LER-IZE.

d: the addictive alkaloid found in tobacco leaves
s: The patch releases a small, steady dose of nicotine through the skin.
r: Named for Jean Nicot (1530-1604), who brought tobacco to the French court
h: NICOTINE ends in -TINE like a sharp little TINE — one C, one T.

d: a climbing vine that hangs in long drooping clusters of purple flowers
s: Purple wisteria spilled over the garden wall every May.
r: Named for Caspar Wistar (1761-1818), American anatomist
h: WISTERIA swaps the man's A for an E — WIST-ERIA.

d: espresso lengthened with hot water
s: He ordered an americano and sat down by the window.
r: Italian for 'American' — GIs in Italy watered espresso down to taste like home
h: AMERICANO is AMERICAN plus O — nothing doubled.

d: a ballpoint pen
s: She scribbled the address with a leaky biro.
r: Named for Laszlo Biro (1899-1985), inventor of the ballpoint pen
h: BIRO rhymes with GYRO and is just as short — four letters, no double R.

d: airtight plastic containers for storing food
s: The leftovers went straight into the tupperware.
r: Named for Earl Tupper (1907-1983), who invented the airtight seal
h: TUPPERWARE doubles the P like SUPPER — supper leftovers in TUPPER-ware.

d: a bath fitted with jets that swirl the water
s: The hotel had a small jacuzzi on the roof terrace.
r: Named for Candido Jacuzzi (1903-1986), who built a hydrotherapy pump for his son
h: JACUZZI doubles the Z and ends in I — Italian, like PIZZA.

d: endless and futile however hard you work at it
s: Clearing sand off the path in a gale was a sisyphean task.
r: From Sisyphus, condemned to roll a boulder uphill forever
h: SISYPHEAN takes the Greek PH and a Y in the middle — SIS-Y-PHEAN, rolling on and on.

d: relating to a child's unconscious rivalry with the same-sex parent
s: The critic read the whole novel as an oedipal struggle.
r: From Oedipus, who unknowingly killed his father and married his mother
h: OEDIPAL opens with the Greek OE pair — never a bare E.

d: forcing everything into one rigid pattern regardless of fit
s: The new timetable was procrustean, and nobody's lessons fitted it.
r: From Procrustes, who stretched or cut travellers to fit his iron bed
h: PROCRUSTEAN hides CRUST in the middle — PRO-CRUST-EAN.

d: a strong painkilling drug made from opium
s: The nurse checked the morphine dose twice before giving it.
r: Named for Morpheus, Greek god of dreams, because the drug brings sleep
h: MORPHINE keeps the PH of MORPHEUS — the dream god is inside the word.

d: an older name for a disorganized form of schizophrenia beginning in youth
s: Nineteenth-century casebooks list the diagnosis as hebephrenia.
r: From Hebe, Greek goddess of youth, plus phren = mind
h: HEBEPHRENIA = HEBE + PHREN — youth plus mind, both spelled the Greek way.

d: having to do with doctors and the practice of medicine
s: He spoke of his esculapian duties with great seriousness.
r: From Aesculapius, Roman god of healing
h: ESCULAPIAN starts ESCU- like ESCAPE with a U.

d: the discarded theory that traits gained in a lifetime pass to offspring
s: The textbook contrasts natural selection with lamarckism.
r: Named for Jean-Baptiste Lamarck (1744-1829)
h: LAMARCKISM keeps the CK of the French name — LA-MARCK-ISM.

d: relating to learning shaped by reward and punishment
s: The training programme was strictly skinnerian.
r: Named for B. F. Skinner (1904-1990), who developed operant conditioning
h: SKINNERIAN doubles the N like DINNER — SKIN-NER-IAN.

d: a number sequence in which each term is the sum of the two before it
s: Sunflower seeds spiral in fibonacci numbers.
r: Named for Leonardo of Pisa, called Fibonacci (c.1170-1250)
h: FIBONACCI doubles the C before the I — Italian, like CAPPUCCINO.

d: a differential operator that sums the second derivatives of a function
s: The equation simplifies once you take the laplacian.
r: Named for Pierre-Simon Laplace (1749-1827)
h: LAPLACIAN keeps PLACE inside it — LA-PLAC-IAN.

d: relating to the economics of comparative advantage and rent
s: Her thesis takes a ricardian view of trade.
r: Named for David Ricardo (1772-1823)
h: RICARDIAN is RICARDO with -IAN, dropping the O.

d: the doctrine of permanent worldwide revolution
s: The pamphlet defends trotskyism against its critics.
r: Named for Leon Trotsky (1879-1940)
h: TROTSKYISM keeps the Y before -ISM — TROT-SKY-ISM.

d: a policy of privatisation, deregulation and free markets
s: The chapter traces the long shadow of thatcherism.
r: Named for Margaret Thatcher (1925-2013)
h: THATCHERISM begins with THATCH like a thatched roof.

d: authoritarian rule justified by popular acclaim and military glory
s: Historians still argue about the appeal of bonapartism.
r: Named for Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821)
h: BONAPARTISM = BONA + PART + ISM.

d: a person who stays cheerful no matter how bad things get
s: Don't be such a pollyanna about the weather.
r: From the relentlessly optimistic heroine of Eleanor Porter's 1913 novel
h: POLLYANNA doubles both the L and the N — POLLY plus ANNA, two names.

d: someone who controls another person through sinister influence
s: The press cast her manager as a svengali.
r: From the hypnotist in George du Maurier's 1894 novel Trilby
h: SVENGALI starts with the odd SV pair — no vowel between S and V.

d: cheerfully certain that everything is for the best
s: His panglossian forecast ignored every warning sign.
r: From Dr Pangloss in Voltaire's Candide
h: PANGLOSSIAN doubles the S — PAN + GLOSS + IAN, all shine.

d: relating to the scholastic philosophy that joins Aristotle to Christian doctrine
s: The seminar opened with a thomistic argument.
r: Named for Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274)
h: THOMISTIC keeps the TH of THOMAS though it sounds like a plain T.

d: the killing of someone by a mob acting without a trial
s: The museum documents every lynching recorded in the county.
r: From Lynch's Law, extrajudicial punishment named for an 18th-century Virginian
h: LYNCHING uses Y where you expect I — L-Y-N-C-H.

d: a machine with a heavy falling blade used for beheading
s: The museum keeps a model guillotine behind glass.
r: Named for Joseph-Ignace Guillotin (1738-1814), who urged a swifter method
h: GUILLOTINE opens like QUILL with a G, doubles the L, and ends -OTINE.

d: belonging to the royal line of the biblical shepherd-king
s: The genealogy traces a davidic descent.
r: From King David of Israel
h: DAVIDIC is the king's name plus -IC — no E anywhere.

d: deliberately obscure or open to more than one reading
s: The minister gave a delphic answer that satisfied nobody.
r: From Delphi, whose oracle spoke in riddles
h: DELPHIC uses PH for the F sound — DEL-PHIC, like DOLPHIN.

d: relating to the first man, or to humankind in its earliest state
s: The poem imagines an adamic innocence before language.
r: From Adam, the first man in Genesis
h: ADAMIC has one D and one M.

d: a woman who has repented and reformed
s: The charity opened as a refuge and called itself a magdalen house.
r: From Mary Magdalene, long identified in tradition with a penitent woman
h: MAGDALEN ends -LEN, not -LIN.

d: a member of an aristocratic Jewish party of the Second Temple period
s: A sadducee denied the resurrection of the dead.
r: From the Hebrew name Zadok, a priestly line
h: SADDUCEE doubles the D and finishes with a double E.

d: the philosophy of suspending judgement about everything
s: His pyrrhonism made him doubt even his own doubts.
r: Named for Pyrrho of Elis (c.360-270 BC), founder of Greek scepticism
h: PYRRHONISM doubles the R and adds a Greek H — PYR-RHO-NISM.

d: based on the ancient theory that health depends on four bodily humours
s: Medieval doctors followed galenic principles for centuries.
r: Named for Galen of Pergamon (129-c.216), physician to Roman emperors
h: GALENIC has a single L.

d: showing the tremor, stiffness and slow movement of a well-known nerve disease
s: The patient's parkinsonian tremor eased with treatment.
r: Named for James Parkinson (1755-1824), who described the shaking palsy
h: PARKINSONIAN = PARK + IN + SON + IAN.

d: extremely loud and powerful, of a voice
s: His stentorian shout carried across the whole field.
r: From Stentor, the Greek herald whose voice Homer said equalled fifty men
h: STENTORIAN begins STEN- not STAN-, and holds a TOR in the middle.

d: fond of luxury and easy pleasure
s: They lived a sybaritic life of long lunches and later mornings.
r: From Sybaris, a Greek colony famed for its luxury
h: SYBARITIC starts with SYB — a Y, not an I.

d: a follower of the philosophy that judges acts by the happiness they produce
s: A strict benthamite would weigh the outcomes and nothing else.
r: Named for Jeremy Bentham (1748-1832), founder of utilitarianism
h: BENTHAMITE keeps the TH before -ITE.

d: a habit of imagining oneself grander and more romantic than one is
s: The novel is a study in bovarism.
r: From Emma Bovary in Flaubert's Madame Bovary
h: BOVARISM trades the heroine's Y for -ISM.

d: bewitching in a way that degrades the person enchanted
s: He warned of the circean pull of easy money.
r: From Circe, who turned Odysseus's crew into pigs
h: CIRCEAN has a soft C twice — CIR-CE-AN.

d: the theory that myths began as exaggerated accounts of real people
s: His reading of the legend is pure euhemerism.
r: Named for Euhemerus (4th century BC), who said the gods were once kings
h: EUHEMERISM opens EU- then H — EU-HEM-ER-ISM.

d: jovial, stout and cheerfully disreputable
s: He had a falstaffian laugh you could hear two rooms away.
r: From Sir John Falstaff in Shakespeare's Henry IV
h: FALSTAFFIAN doubles the F — FAL-STAFF-IAN, a big man with a big staff.

d: keenly observant and given to reasoning from tiny details
s: She made a holmesian deduction from a scuff on his shoe.
r: From Sherlock Holmes, Arthur Conan Doyle's detective
h: HOLMESIAN keeps the silent L of the detective's name.

d: a person who betrays a friend or a cause
s: The play brands him an iscariot to his own people.
r: From Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver
h: ISCARIOT holds a CAR in the middle — IS-CAR-I-OT.

d: a cold and calculating schemer
s: Every court in the play has its machiavel.
r: From Niccolo Machiavelli (1469-1527), author of The Prince
h: MACHIAVEL uses CH for a hard K — MA-CHI-A-VEL.

d: a comic slip in which a similar-sounding wrong word is used
s: He produced a splendid malapropism, praising her fine constellation of manners.
r: From Mrs Malaprop in Sheridan's The Rivals; French mal a propos = out of place
h: MALAPROPISM = MAL + A + PROP + ISM — the wrong word propped in place.

d: marked by long wandering and survival through cleverness
s: Their odyssean journey home took most of a year.
r: From Odysseus, ten years sailing home from Troy
h: ODYSSEAN doubles the S and uses Y — OD-YS-SE-AN.

d: boisterously earthy and exuberant in humour
s: The feast scene is rabelaisian in its excess.
r: From Francois Rabelais (c.1494-1553), author of Gargantua and Pantagruel
h: RABELAISIAN keeps the French AI — RAB-E-LAIS-IAN.

d: favouring tradition and slow, cautious reform
s: He made a burkean case against sudden change.
r: Named for Edmund Burke (1729-1797)
h: BURKEAN keeps the E of the name before -AN.

d: belonging to a golden age of art and public building
s: The museum's collection is strongest on periclean sculpture.
r: Named for Pericles (c.495-429 BC), who led Athens at its height
h: PERICLEAN hides CLEAN at the end — PERI-CLEAN.

d: written in a four-line stanza of a particular ancient Greek pattern
s: She translated the ode into sapphic stanzas.
r: Named for Sappho of Lesbos (c.630-570 BC)
h: SAPPHIC doubles the P and then adds H — SAP-PHIC.

d: rational, ordered and serene
s: The building's apollonian calm makes the square feel larger.
r: From Apollo, god of light, reason and proportion
h: APOLLONIAN doubles the L — A-POL-LO-NI-AN.

d: describing a victory that ruins the winner
s: Taking the hill was a cadmean success; half the company was lost.
r: From Cadmus, whose sown dragon's teeth sprang up as warriors who killed each other
h: CADMEAN is CAD plus MEAN.

d: secret and known only to those initiated
s: The society guarded its rules with eleusinian care.
r: From Eleusis, home of the secret mysteries of Demeter
h: ELEUSINIAN carries the Greek EU in the middle — E-LEU-SIN-IAN.

d: of a deep purplish blue, or of thick curling hair
s: The painter gave the boy hyacinthine curls.
r: From Hyacinthus, from whose blood Apollo raised a flower
h: HYACINTHINE keeps the Y and the TH — HY-A-CIN-THINE.

d: causing forgetfulness
s: He drank a lethean draught and remembered nothing.
r: From Lethe, the underworld river of forgetting
h: LETHEAN has TH in the middle — LE-THE-AN.

d: having to do with dancing
s: Her terpsichorean skill won the whole hall over.
r: From Terpsichore, Muse of dance, whose name means 'delighting in dance'
h: TERPSICHOREAN hides CHOR, like CHOIR — TERP-SI-CHOR-EAN.

d: having to do with volcanoes or with working metal
s: The forge glowed with vulcanian heat.
r: From Vulcan, Roman god of the forge, whose workshop lay under Etna
h: VULCANIAN uses a C, never a K.

d: wildly ecstatic and uninhibited
s: The final dance became dionysiac.
r: From Dionysus, god of wine and of the festivals that produced Greek drama
h: DIONYSIAC uses Y for the third vowel — DI-O-NY-SI-AC.

d: to paralyse someone with a terrifying stare
s: One look from the headmaster could gorgonize a whole corridor.
r: From the Gorgons, whose gaze turned people to stone
h: GORGONIZE has two O's and no A.

d: relating to nineteenth-century Irish republican nationalism
s: The pamphlet was seized as fenian propaganda.
r: From the Fianna, the warrior bands of Irish legend
h: FENIAN begins FEN- like a marshy FEN.

d: belonging to a stern puritan republican rule
s: The chapel still has its bare cromwellian windows.
r: Named for Oliver Cromwell (1599-1658), Lord Protector of England
h: CROMWELLIAN doubles the L — there is a WELL inside it.

d: generous in appearance but giving nothing at all
s: The offer turned out to be barmecidal.
r: From the Barmecide, who served a beggar a banquet of empty dishes
h: BARMECIDAL takes a soft C in the middle — BAR-ME-CI-DAL.

d: relating to extravagant gourmet cooking
s: The menu had apician ambitions and a very long bill.
r: Named for Apicius, the Roman gourmet whose name is on the West's oldest cookbook
h: APICIAN ends -CIAN like MUSICIAN.

d: belonging to the calm high point of the Roman Empire
s: The wall marks the antonine frontier.
r: Named for Antoninus Pius (86-161), whose reign was famously peaceful
h: ANTONINE ends -NINE, like the number.

d: living alone and withdrawn from the world, like a hermit
s: He took up an anchoretic life in a hut on the moor.
r: From Greek anachoretes = one who withdraws, used of the desert hermits
h: ANCHORETIC hides ANCHOR — the hermit anchored in the desert.

d: of a fourteen-line love poem split into an eight-line and a six-line part
s: She wrote the whole sequence in petrarchan form.
r: Named for Petrarch (1304-1374), who wrote hundreds of sonnets to Laura
h: PETRARCHAN uses CH for a hard K — PE-TRAR-CHAN.

d: a story about surviving alone on a desert island
s: The novel is a robinsonade set in the Arctic.
r: From Robinson Crusoe, whose many imitators created the genre
h: ROBINSONADE ends -ADE, like a drink named after him.

d: a strong blue cheese made from sheep's milk
s: He crumbled roquefort over the sliced pears.
r: Named for Roquefort-sur-Soulzon, where the cheese ripens in limestone caves
h: ROQUEFORT uses the French QUE and ends in a silent T.

d: a fine bobbin lace with a diamond-shaped mesh
s: The cuffs were trimmed with valenciennes.
r: Named for Valenciennes in northern France
h: VALENCIENNES doubles the N near the end and keeps a silent S.

d: a soft white mineral carved into tobacco pipes
s: His grandfather's meerschaum pipe had darkened to amber.
r: German for 'sea foam' — the stone is so light that it floats
h: MEERSCHAUM carries the German SCH and AU — MEER-SCHAUM.

d: a soft cheese with a strong smell and an orange rind
s: A wedge of munster cleared the room.
r: Named for Munster in Alsace, from Latin monasterium = monastery
h: MUNSTER starts MUN-, not MON-.

d: a deep purplish pink
s: The dye came out a startling solferino.
r: Named for the 1859 battle of Solferino, fought the year the dye appeared
h: SOLFERINO = SOL + FER + INO, with a single L.

d: a coarse ribbed woollen cloth
s: The coat was cut from heavy kersey.
r: Named for the Suffolk village of Kersey, weaving it since the 1300s
h: KERSEY ends -SEY like JERSEY, another cloth named after a place.

d: strips of hair grown down the sides of the face in front of the ears
s: He grew enormous sideburns for the school play.
r: From General Ambrose Burnside, whose whiskers were called burnsides until the halves were swapped
h: SIDEBURNS is the general's name turned back to front.

d: pleasure taken in causing pain to others
s: The report described casual sadism in the camp.
r: Named for the Marquis de Sade (1740-1814)
h: SADISM has a single D.

d: pleasure taken in one's own pain or humiliation
s: Running that hill twice was pure masochism.
r: Named for Leopold von Sacher-Masoch (1836-1895), author of Venus in Furs
h: MASOCHISM keeps a CH that sounds like K.

d: a pizza topped with tomato, mozzarella and basil
s: She ordered a margherita and ate the whole thing.
r: Named for Queen Margherita of Savoy, served a pizza in the colours of the Italian flag
h: MARGHERITA hides a silent H after the G — MAR-GHE-RI-TA.

d: a bottle of petrol used as a hand-thrown firebomb
s: The museum displays a molotov from the winter war.
r: Named mockingly for Vyacheslav Molotov (1890-1986) by Finnish soldiers
h: MOLOTOV has three O's and ends in V, not F.

d: a dark red fruit crossed from a blackberry and a raspberry
s: The loganberry jam was almost too sharp.
r: Named for James Harvey Logan (1841-1928), who crossed the two plants by accident
h: LOGANBERRY doubles the R at the end.

d: an electronic instrument played by moving the hands near two antennas
s: The eerie whine in the film score is a theremin.
r: Named for Leon Theremin (1896-1993), who invented it in 1920
h: THEREMIN starts with THERE — the instrument you play from over there.

d: a concert grand piano of a celebrated make
s: The hall keeps a steinway on stage all year.
r: From Heinrich Steinweg, who anglicised his name after emigrating to New York
h: STEINWAY uses the German EI — STEIN, like a beer stein, then WAY.

d: an early voltage-controlled electronic music synthesizer
s: The band's whole sound came out of one moog.
r: Named for Robert Moog (1934-2005), who built the first widely used synthesizer
h: MOOG has two O's like MOON and ends in a hard G.

d: a rare potassium mineral found near volcanic vents
s: A few crystals of avogadrite were collected on the crater rim.
r: Named for Amedeo Avogadro (1776-1856)
h: AVOGADRITE is the chemist's name with -ITE for a mineral.
